evidence: Sound system exclusivity, and the one-off acetate as the object that carries it, are described throughout histories of Jamaican music. Commissioned unique mixes for named sound systems are described as the economic basis of the work done at Tubby's studio, not a side effect of it. Held at consensus because no first-hand source is named here (Q22).

later.title: dub mixes cut for named sound systems

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Listen for who the record is talking to. A sound system's name gets shouted over the top of the mix, or the singer greets a crew by name, and you realise the record is not addressed to you or to a radio audience. It was made for one crowd in one yard on one night, on a disc that would be worn out within a few months.

explanation: Before pressing thousands of copies you would cut one soft disc and try it at a dance. Then people worked out that the one-copy part was the valuable bit: if only your sound system has a record, nobody can beat you with it. So sound systems competing paid engineers to cut special versions all night, often with a crew's name shouted over the top, and that steady paid demand for one-off mixes funded the studio hours in which dub's techniques were worked out. It is the money underneath dub. It also turns recording upside down: the disc is valuable because it cannot be copied, and since it wears out after fifty or a hundred plays, it was all meant to be temporary.
